name: Myanmar
sources: READ THIS FIRST — THE GDP FIGURE DEPARTS FROM THIS ROSTER'S USUAL SERIES AND THE REASON IS STATED IN FULL. Every other nation here takes gdp_bn from World Bank NY.GDP.MKTP.CD. That series gives Myanmar 1990 = $2,115,193,513. It is not entered, and this is the disagreement, laid out rather than split: $2.115bn over 39.8m people is $53 per head, which would make Myanmar the poorest place on earth by a factor of several and would rank it in this game BELOW Nepal, whose economy the same series values at $3.63bn for half the population. No source of any kind holds that Nepal's 1990 output exceeded Burma's. The number is an exchange-rate artefact, and the arithmetic that proves it is in this file: the World Bank's own DT.DOD.DECT.GN.ZS gives Myanmar external debt at 254.13% of GNI for 1990, which against $2.1bn implies a debt stock of about $5.3bn — and the CIA World Factbook 1990 states 'External debt: $5.6 billion (December 1989 est.)'. The two sources agree almost exactly on the DEBT in dollars and disagree fivefold on the GDP. The denominator is what is broken, not the numerator.

GDP $11.0bn: CIA World Factbook 1990, Burma entry, verbatim — 'GDP: $11.0 billion, per capita $280; real growth rate 0.2% (FY88 est.)'. This is the kyat figure converted at the official rate, which the same entry gives as 'kyats (K) per US$1—6.5188 (January 1990)'. THE OFFICIAL RATE WAS ITSELF A FICTION, overvaluing the kyat by roughly an order of magnitude against the parallel market, so $11.0bn is the high end of a range whose low end is the World Bank's $2.1bn and whose truth is neither. IT IS ENTERED ANYWAY, for one reason: it is the figure that keeps this roster internally coherent per head. $11.0bn over 39.8m is $276, against Bangladesh's $283 in this same roster from a completely independent source. Two of the poorest large economies in Asia, entered from two different sources, landing within 3% of each other per capita, is a far better cross-check than a number that says Burma was one fifth as rich as Nepal. Myanmar's GDP is listed as UNVERIFIED in this region's report and it should be treated as the weakest headline figure on the board.

Population 39.8m: World Bank SP.POP.TOTL, series MMR, 1990 = 39,817,251. The CIA World Factbook 1990 gives 41,277,389 for July 1990. The World Bank figure is entered because population, unlike GDP, is on the same series as the rest of this roster, and the 3.5% gap between the two is ordinary census uncertainty rather than the structural problem the GDP line has.

TFP trend 0.004: the Burmese Way to Socialism had run the country into applying for United Nations Least Developed Country status in 1987 — a formal admission of failure by a state that had been among the richest in Southeast Asia at independence. SLORC began opening the economy after the 1988 coup, with the Foreign Investment Law of 30 November 1988, but in January 1990 almost nothing had arrived. Set above Afghanistan's 0.002 floor and below Nepal's 0.006.

Inflation 17.6%: World Bank FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG, series MMR, 1990 = 17.63%. Entered from the World Bank because it is a price index rather than a dollar conversion and therefore does not carry the exchange-rate problem that disqualified the GDP line. The CIA World Factbook 1990 gives 22.6% for FY89, a different fiscal period; the discrepancy is noted rather than averaged. Behind both is the demonetisation of 5 September 1987, which voided about 80% of the currency in circulation without compensation, wiped out household savings and triggered the protests that became the 1988 uprising.

Interest rate 12%: NOT A TRANSCRIBED SERIES and flagged unverified. World Bank FR.INR.LEND returns null for Myanmar for 1990. Rates in Burma were administered by the state banking monopoly rather than set by any market, with deposit and lending rates fixed in the low teens. 12% against 17.6% inflation gives a real rate near minus 5.5%, which is the correct shape for a socialist banking system with a state deficit behind it, and sits comfortably inside this schema's coupled real-rate constraint.

Revenue 6.2% of GDP: World Bank GC.TAX.TOTL.GD.ZS, series MMR, 1990 = 6.20%. A real observation. CAVEAT, since it is a ratio and this file has just rejected the denominator: this indicator is computed in local currency and is therefore unaffected by the kyat conversion problem, which is precisely why it is safe to use here when the dollar GDP was not.

Military 3.4% of GDP and a strength index of 6: World Bank MS.MIL.XPND.GD.ZS, series MMR, 1990 = 3.396%, also a local-currency ratio and so also unaffected by the exchange rate. It cross-checks against the CIA World Factbook 1990 line 'Defense expenditures: $315.0 million, 21.0% of central government budget (FY88)' — $315m against $11.0bn GDP is 2.9%, close to the World Bank's 3.4% and further evidence that $11.0bn is the coherent denominator. The Tatmadaw numbered roughly 230,000 in 1990 and was doubling. Strength 6 is indexed above Bangladesh's 4 — more than twice the manpower, similar dollars, and continuously in combat since 1948 — and well below Pakistan's 16, which had an air force and armour Burma did not.

Public investment 8% and private investment 5% of GDP: A JUDGEMENT. World Bank NE.GDI.TOTL.ZS returns null for Myanmar for 1990. Burma's investment rate was in the low teens as a share of GDP and overwhelmingly state, since the private sector had been nationalised in 1963 and was only beginning to be tolerated again. The 13% total and the state-heavy split are the shape of a command economy at the start of a grudging opening, and neither half is a measurement.

Debt 51% of GDP: CIA World Factbook 1990 — 'External debt: $5.6 billion (December 1989 est.)' — against the same source's $11.0bn GDP. Same stated substitution as the rest of this region: this schema's field means gross public debt and external debt is what exists. The World Bank's 254% of GNI for the same debt stock is not a disagreement about Burma's borrowing, it is the same $5.6bn divided by the $2.1bn GDP this file has already explained, and it is quoted here because it is the cleanest single demonstration of why that denominator was rejected.

Oil 0.01 mbd: Burma produced roughly ten thousand barrels a day from the old Yenangyaung and Mann fields and was a net importer of petroleum products despite having been an oil exporter under the Raj. Entered at the resolution this field permits. The gas that later mattered — Yadana, Yetagun — was not discovered until the 1990s and must not be written into a 1990 start.

Stability 38 and authoritarianism 0.90: January 1990 sits between two events that define the entry. The 8888 uprising had been put down on 18 September 1988 by a coup that killed in the thousands and installed the State Law and Order Restoration Council; Aung San Suu Kyi had been under house arrest since 20 July 1989; and on 27 May 1990 SLORC held a general election, lost it catastrophically, and annulled the result. Stability 38 is set above Afghanistan's 25 and Nigeria's 35 and below Yugoslavia's 44 — a regime with essentially no legitimacy and overwhelming coercive capacity, which is a different thing from a regime about to fall, and the proof is that it governed for twenty-one more years. Authoritarianism 0.90 sits level with China, above Iran's 0.85 and below Vietnam's 0.92.

Separatism 0.45: the highest figure in this roster outside Yugoslavia's 0.72, above Sri Lanka's 0.40 and Turkey's 0.30. Myanmar in 1990 held the longest continuously running civil war in the world, begun in 1948, and it was not one insurgency but a dozen simultaneous ones holding real territory: the Karen National Union administering Manerplaw as a capital, the Kachin Independence Army in the north, Shan and Mon and Karenni fronts, and — new and enormous — the United Wa State Army and the other forces created when the rank and file of the Communist Party of Burma mutinied against their leadership in March and April 1989 and split along ethnic lines. The ceasefires SLORC began signing with those groups from 1989 are the reason this is 0.45 and not higher: the state was buying the frontier rather than holding it, which is a real and unstable arrangement rather than an ongoing collapse.

pop_growth_1990 = 1.7823%/yr. Compound annual growth of World Bank SP.POP.TOTL, series MMR (Myanmar): 35,899,313 in 1984 to 39,214,618 in 1989 — the five years ending on the eve of the 1 January 1990 start date. See EconomyRecord::pop_growth_1990 in spheres-sim/src/data/mod.rs for why the window ends in 1989 and not with the single-year 1990 rate.

note: 1990 TECHNOLOGY: AUTHORED, NOT DERIVED. What this nation knew on 1 January 1990 is transcribed and sourced grant by grant, exactly like every other 1990 figure in this file, and is not read off tfp_trend - there was never a code path from the trend to the known set, and the zero that stood there was a claim about the world rather than an absence of one (BIBLE section 8 and iron rule 4, both amended 2026-08-30). THE PREDICATE IS SPLIT, and split by the technology's OWN EFFECT TYPE so that it is mechanically computable and never a per-nation judgement call. A node whose effects include MilitaryEfficiency, MilitaryStrength, DiffusionEmission or CostReduction is SOVEREIGNTY-SIDE: holding it means this nation could PRODUCE it, so operating an imported article does not qualify. Every other node is USE-SIDE: deployed and in operational use here is enough, whoever built it, because the effect such a node pays is a productivity, health or output effect and that effect is real in the country where the machine runs. Of the 48 technologies the tree lets anyone hold in 1990, 17 are sovereignty-side and 31 are use-side.

DATA-KEYED TAIL NATION. This nation is outside the 29 authored majors, so nothing here was authored technology by technology: a grant is made only where one of two named published global series supports it, and nothing is modelled, estimated or interpolated. A short list, or an empty one, is the correct outcome of that rule and not a gap in the work.

Data-keyed tail nation: not one of the 29 authored majors. Only the two series named in ruling 3 were consulted - WHO/UNICEF WUENIC DTP3 1990 and World Bank IT.CEL.SETS. Nothing was modelled, estimated or interpolated, and no other evidence was admitted. ISO3 key used for both series: MMR.
WUENIC DTP3 1990 = 88% against the 80% UCI-1990 threshold: bio_universal_immunisation GRANTED.
IT.CEL.SETS at 31 December 1989 = 0 against a threshold of any positive count: refused.

The other 46 grantable 1990 technologies are BLANK for this nation by design, not by oversight: the 17 sovereignty-side entries are unreachable by any use-in-operation series, and no published global series was named that keys the remaining 29 use-side entries.

granted.source: WHO/UNICEF WUENIC DTP3 immunisation coverage (% of surviving infants), retrieved from the UNICEF public SDMX API, dataflow UNICEF:IMMUNISATION(1.0), indicator IM_DTP3, DATA_SOURCE field 'WHO/UNICEF estimates of national immunization coverage, 2025 revision'. Series value: MMR, 1990 = 88%, at or above the 80% WHO/UNICEF Universal Childhood Immunization (UCI-1990) target that defines this technology's name. The 1989 value of the same series is 50%, on the other side of the 80% line: THRESHOLD-SENSITIVE CELL.
